name: Rhubarb diet

lead: The rhubarb diet is a short-term plan in which stewed rhubarb takes the place of regular meals, commonly described as paired with milk or dairy. People try it to lose weight and look slimmer.
Rhubarb stalks are low in calories, about 21 kcal per 100 g raw. Rhubarb root has a long history in traditional Chinese medicine as a laxative. No clinical trial of a rhubarb diet was found.

paras: Descriptions of the plan have people eating stewed rhubarb, often with dairy, in place of some meals for a short period. It is typically a temporary approach rather than a long-term eating pattern.

Rhubarb stalks contain oxalic acid, and long-term high intake can contribute to kidney stones; leaves are poisonous. The anthraquinones in rhubarb roots and stems are laxative, and long-term consumption has been associated with kidney failure. Anyone with kidney problems should seek medical advice first.

angle.text: Followers use rhubarb in place of regular meals to cut calories for a short period. Any weight lost reflects lower intake and, according to the Wikipedia rhubarb article, laxative compounds.

lead: The rhubarb diet is a fad eating plan centered on stewed rhubarb, used for weight loss. Rhubarb stalks are very low in energy at about 21 kcal per 100 g raw, and are 94 percent water, which is the basis of the plan's appeal for people who want to slim down.[1]

Rhubarb has an older reputation as a medicine. Its root appears in the Shennong Ben Cao Jing, thought to date back about 1,800 years, and in traditional Chinese medicine it was used as a laxative for millennia.[1] No published clinical trial of the diet was found.

paras: Raw rhubarb provides 21 kcal per 100 g, with 1.8 g fiber and 24 percent of the daily value for vitamin K, and moderate potassium.[1] Stalks are the edible part and are most often cooked with sugar.[1]

In Chinese medicine the root, known as dà huáng, was used as a laxative; Wikipedia states there is no clinical evidence that this use is effective.[1] Rhubarb reached Europe along the Silk Road, with Russian rhubarb valued most in medieval Europe.[1]

Leaves contain high levels of oxalic acid and anthrone glycosides and are poisonous. Oxalic acid is a nephrotoxin, and long-term consumption can lead to kidney stones.[1] Roots and stems contain anthraquinones such as emodin; long-term anthraquinone consumption has been associated with acute kidney failure.[1]
